units.signature: fn clamp(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> [] int
units.description: Limit x to the range lo..hi: lo if x < lo, hi if x > hi, otherwise x. The caller guarantees lo <= hi (lo == hi is allowed and then the answer is that value). Any x is allowed, including the extremes of int. Never panics.

units.signature: fn gcd(a: int, b: int) -> [] int
units.description: The greatest common divisor of a and b, always >= 0: the sign of a and of b never matters. gcd(a, 0) and gcd(0, a) are |a|, and gcd(0, 0) is 0. Domain: |a| <= 4611686018427387904 (2^62) and |b| <= 4611686018427387904; no operation may overflow inside it. int is 64-bit and overflow is an error, not a wrap.

units.signature: fn lcm(a: int, b: int) -> [] int
units.description: The least common multiple, always >= 0, sign ignored like gcd. It is 0 if either argument is 0. Domain: |a| <= 3000000000 and |b| <= 3000000000, so the result always fits an int. Use gcd.

The proleptic Gregorian rule applied to the integer y exactly as given: a leap year is divisible by 4, except that a year divisible by 100 is not, unless it is also divisible by 400. Domain: any int, negative years and 0 included (year 0 is a leap year, -4 is a leap year, -100 is not). Beware: % on a negative int can be negative; compare it with == 0 only.

The integer square root floor(sqrt(n)): the largest r with r * r <= n. Domain: 0 <= n <= 9223372036854775807, exact for the whole range. r * r and (r + 1) * (r + 1) can overflow near the top of the range (the answer there is 3037000499, whose square fits but whose successor's square does not), and a floating point square root is not exact there; compare with a division, or bound the search. n < 0 is outside the domain.

units.signature: fn pow_mod(base: int, exp: int, modulus: int) -> [] int
units.description: base to the power exp, modulo modulus, always in 0 .. modulus - 1 (a negative base still gives a non-negative answer). pow_mod(b, 0, m) is 1 % m, so it is 0 when m is 1. Domain: |base| <= 4611686018427387904, 0 <= exp <= 4611686018427387904, 1 <= modulus <= 3000000000. The power itself is far too large to compute: reduce as you go (square and multiply), so that no intermediate value overflows the 64-bit int.
